The Story of Revati

I pay homage to the Jina who benefits all the world, and write here the story of Queen Revati, who practiced amudh-drishti — undeluded vision, the limb of right faith that sees through illusion.

In the beautiful city of Meghkut, on the southern range of the Vijyardh mountains, there ruled a king named Chandraprabh. He governed happily for many years until one day a desire for pilgrimage arose in his heart. Entrusting his kingdom to his son Chandrashekhar, he set out on his journey.

Travelling to South Mathura, he had the good fortune to meet Acharya Guptacharya. The king listened to the acharya's discourse and was profoundly moved. Understanding that service to others is the greatest merit on earth, he renounced his royal life and became a kshullak — a junior ascetic — retaining one spiritual practice for his pilgrimages.

The Guru's Message

One day he wished to travel to North Mathura. Before departing, he asked his guru, "Master, do you have any message I should carry for anyone?" Guptacharya replied, "In Mathura there is a wise monk named Surat. Carry my greetings to him. And to the virtuous Queen Revati, convey my blessings for her spiritual growth." The kshullak asked if there was anyone else, but the acharya said no.

Chandraprabh wondered why the guru had sent greetings only to Surat Muni and Revati, passing over even the learned Bhavyasen and other monks. He set out anyway, trusting that the reason would reveal itself in time.

Arriving in North Mathura, he delivered the guru's greetings to Surat Muni, who received him with great warmth and fraternal love. Then he visited Bhavyasen, the scholar of the eleven scriptures. But Bhavyasen, swollen with pride, did not even return the greeting. Such is the curse of arrogance — even learning cannot purify a heart that clings to vanity.

Testing the Proud Monk

Curious about Bhavyasen, Chandraprabh followed him the next morning. Using his spiritual powers, he made the ground ahead lush and green with tender grass. Bhavyasen walked right over it, thinking, "Our scriptures call these single-sensed beings — the harm is minimal." When the monk finished his ablutions, he found his water pot empty and overturned. Chandraprabh had dried it with his powers. He pointed out a nearby lake, and Bhavyasen went to fill his pot there — violating his own vows about proper water sources.

Chandraprabh now understood: knowledge without humility is hollow. The acharya had been right to send no greeting to such a one.

Testing Queen Revati

Now Chandraprabh turned his attention to Queen Revati, wife of King Varun of the same city. He decided to test the depth of her faith. On the first day, he used his powers to appear as a great deity in the northern quarter. The whole city rushed to worship. Even the king and Bhavyasen went. But Revati did not go. She knew the true gods, and this was not one of them.

On the second day he appeared as Vishnu, four-armed with conch and discus. On the third day, as Shiva seated on a bull. On the fourth day, he manifested an entire samavasaran — a celestial preaching hall — with a Tirthankara seated within it, attended by thousands of gods.

Everyone marvelled and rushed to pay homage. But Revati remained unmoved. She knew from the scriptures that there are only twenty-four Tirthankaras, nine Vasudevas, and eleven Rudras. No new ones could simply appear. These were illusions, and she would not be deceived. Can the wind move Mount Meru?

The Final Test

At last Chandraprabh came to Revati's door disguised as a wretched, disease-ridden beggar. He collapsed in her courtyard. Revati ran to him, carried him inside, and fed him with her own hands.

Still not satisfied, the ascetic vomited the food back out, producing a terrible stench. Revati felt only sorrow — not disgust. She blamed herself for offering improper food, cleaned his body with warm water, and tended him with pure compassion.

Now Chandraprabh was fully satisfied. He gathered his powers, revealed himself, and blessed her: "Devi, may the spiritual blessings of my guru Guptacharya purify your heart. I tested your undeluded vision in many ways and found you immovable. Who can adequately praise your faith, which is honoured across all three worlds?"

In the fullness of time, King Varun renounced the world, became an ascetic, and attained heaven. Queen Revati took initiation, practiced austerities, and was reborn as a goddess of great power. Those who seek heaven or liberation should follow her example: abandon delusion and embrace the dharma with clear, unwavering eyes.
